terms.grammar: angustiae, plural, “narrows”, with in and the ablative
evidence: Caes. BC 1.54: cum in hīs angustiīs rēs esset (Lewis & Short), s.v. angustiae
terms.comment: The word is the narrows of a pass; transferred, “difficulty, distress, perplexity, straits” (Lewis & Short). To get someone into a fix: in summās angustiās addūcere (Cic. Quinct. 5, Lewis & Short).

sources: Lewis & Short: angustiae · Lewis & Short: versor
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 98, 335.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
